news.title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
paras: A bar of explosive material at an Army plant in Middletown, Iowa, was almost set to explode. The President ordered the plan stopped, saying a judge would decide what happens next. The government said the explosion would send poisonous gas far away, but it was delayed. People in Iowa learned only days before the change, because the Army had not listened to environmental groups. The groups asked a court to stop the blast, and the court agreed. The new governor will decide if the Army should burn them or find a safer method. The military will talk with locals before making another plan.

news.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
paras: Consumer Checkpoint Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more Personalized pricing can mean unfair, and even biased, prices. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history , smart devices , and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

paras: Before New Shepard all boosters were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets.

After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.

news.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
paras: When humans live on the moon, we'll need to grow food on the moon, too. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home.

But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement .

paras: Add as preferred source Salvador Dalí, Untitled , 1931, is among the Surrealist works on view at the Royal Academy’s new exhibition.

Salvador Dalí / Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí / DACS Long before Peggy Guggenheim became synonymous with her palazzo art museum on Venice’s Grand Canal, she launched her art collecting career in a modest storefront on London’s Cork Street. paras: Add as preferred source Restorers are finishing a six-month renovation at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas Church, which will reopen with a celebratory mass on December 15. Scenes portraying both biblical stories and indigenous symbols are the outcome of rare collaborations between Spanish colonizers and native communities in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

This spring, the Vatican restored the Sistine Chapel for the first time in 30 years, including cleansing the sweat of tourists from Michelangelo’s murals and researching the multi-headed brushes that the painter used. “It is a jewel of mestizo Baroque art,” Reverend Jacek Dziadosz , a Polish priest known locally as Father Jacinto, tells Carlos Valdez of the Associated Press (AP).

news.title: What Can 300 Years of European Portraits Reveal About Evolving Beauty Standards?
paras: Add as preferred source Before the Mirror , Pierre-Paul-Léon Glaize, 1873 Public domain via Wikimedia Commons Long before the invention of photography, wealthy Europeans commissioned portraits to preserve their likenesses for posterity. But portraits aren’t necessarily faithful reproductions of reality.

Like photos, they can be manipulated to accentuate flattering features, portraying subjects as they wish to be seen. As it happens, those choices can tell us a great deal about how ideal beauty standards have evolved over time. According to a study published last week in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B , historic portraits serve as “cognitive fossils” that shed new light on “historical shifts in psychological preferences and reproductive strategies.”
